source.title: The Grounding Gap: How LLMs Anchor the Meaning of Abstract Concepts Differently from Humans
source.authors: Odysseas S. Chlapanis; Orfeas Menis-Mastromichalakis; Christos H. Papadimitriou

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether model performance on behavioral evaluation tasks changes with model scale, using human-alignment correlations rather than held-out pretraining loss or scaling-law fits.
record.gate_note: The study measures human–model alignment on property-generation and explicit rating tasks and relates it to parameter count. These are behavioral alignment outcomes, not held-out cross-entropy, fitted loss exponents, compute-optimal allocations, or architecture comparisons. Its scale results bear on V6 only. The cited scaling-law results are background, not results of this study.
record.test_reason: The study reports how a downstream task score (model–human alignment r on property-generation and rating tasks) varies with parameter count across 21 models. That bears on V6 in a new setting. It does not measure loss, fits or allocation. The scale comparison is cross-family and uses estimated sizes for closed models, so it is not a controlled scaling series. T3 fits better than T2 because it is a new task setting, not a different method aimed at the original question.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially right. The authors also conclude that further scaling or text-based training will probably not close the gap on spontaneous generation, because alignment there does not improve with scale.
record.recipe_differences: The study replicates cognitive-science behavioral experiments; it does not use or evaluate the original scaling-law loss-fitting method.
record.method_sensitivity: The scale pattern differs by evaluation task: property-generation alignment shows no reliable improvement or monotonic trend, whereas explicit rating alignment improves with scale. Within the rating task, scale effects vary by component.
record.problems: The outcomes are behavioral human-alignment correlations rather than pretraining loss. Closed-model parameter counts are estimates. The study evaluates 21 models, and its rating-task scale pattern is uneven across components; uncertainties are not given for the aggregate scale trends.
record.rows_left_out: No separate model-by-model rows were extracted for the 21-model tables. The retained rows capture the study's explicitly stated aggregate scale findings for each task; individual scores appear in Appendix B.2 Table 4, Appendix C Table 5, and Appendix D Table 6.

untested.parts: No fitted extrapolation is made from small runs.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, repeated data or transfer power laws.
Downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss is not tested. No controlled single-family scaling series exists beyond 2–3 sizes per open family.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponent setups.

missing.what: Within-family component scaling on the rating task: Sensory improves (Gemma −0.086→0.704; Llama −0.161→0.729; Qwen3 0.321→0.807); Internal and Social are flat; Motor is flat or drops with size
Within-family size comparisons on Experiment 1 (e.g. Gemma 4B 0.270 > 27B 0.196; GPT-OSS 20B 0.302 > 120B 0.199; Llama 8B 0.283 < 70B 0.375)

record.verdict_notes: Scale here is cross-family and uses estimated parameter counts for closed models (Li 2026). All models are instruct-tuned, and training data and compute differ, so scale is confounded with family. The cited Hoffmann et al. result is background only. The SAE and steering results do not bear on any version.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss is measured as a function of parameter count, tokens, or compute.
No small-run power-law fits are used to predict larger-run losses.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameter count and training tokens is evaluated.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count is reported.
No power-law comparison across modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer is performed.

Tests scale-related changes in human-alignment metrics on these behavioral tasks only; it does not test conventional downstream benchmarks against pretraining loss or fit a general predictive scaling relation.
Does not compare loss-law fitting choices, parameter-counting methods, or training schedules, and does not test departures from fitted loss curves.

rows.subject: 21 LLMs (aggregate result reported across the model panel)
rows.size_stated: 21 models spanning several families; sizes vary and include open-weight parameter counts and estimated counts for closed models
rows.stage_stated: instruct for the named instruct/chat models; otherwise not stated
rows.operation_detail: Property generation on the 293-word Harpaintner abstract-noun set; compare model category-frequency profiles with human profiles and examine alignment against model scale.
rows.measure: Mean Pearson r of model–human category-frequency profiles; the paper reports that larger models and stronger general-purpose systems do not show reliably higher human alignment.
rows.value: No reliably higher human alignment with larger models; best model mean r ≈ 0.37; estimated human ceiling about 0.97.
rows.uncertainty: Bootstrap standard deviations over 1000 resamples are reported for selected models; not stated for the aggregate scale finding.
rows.note: Aggregate scale-pattern statement across the panel; individual model scores are also tabulated. The study says the gap is not explained by scale.
rows.check: Link and state are correct. Table 4 shows no size ordering: Llama 3.1 70B is top (0.375) but Gemma-3-27B is last (0.196), below Gemma-3-4B (0.270), and GPT-OSS 120B (0.199) is below GPT-OSS 20B (0.302). Within some families the trend is reversed.

rows.subject: 21 LLMs (aggregate result reported across the model panel)
rows.size_stated: 21 models spanning several families; sizes vary and include open-weight parameter counts and estimated counts for closed models
rows.stage_stated: instruct for the named instruct/chat models; otherwise not stated
rows.operation_detail: Property generation on the combined abstract subset from the Kelly et al. experiment; compare model category-frequency profiles with human profiles and examine the relation to model scale.

conditions.value: 236 abstract words: emotion and non-emotion items combined

rows.measure: Mean Pearson r of model–human category-frequency profiles; the paper reports no monotonic trend in parameter count.
rows.value: No monotonic trend in parameter count; strongest models reach only mean r ≈ 0.33 in the main text (Appendix B reports ≈ 0.36). Human-to-human correlation is about 0.91.
rows.uncertainty: Table 5 reports ± values for individual model correlations; not stated for the aggregate scale-pattern statement.
rows.locator: Section 3.2 and Appendix C, Figure 7 and Table 5
rows.note: The appendix gives a strongest-model value of ≈0.36 for this subset, while the main text says ≈0.33; both state that alignment is low and the scale trend is not monotonic.
rows.check: Link and state are correct. The best abstract score in Table 5 is 0.361 (Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite), so the appendix figure of ≈0.36 matches the table; the main text's ≈0.33 is inconsistent with it. Small models (Gemma 3 12B 0.348, Gemma 3 4B 0.309) outrank large ones (Gemini 3.1 Pro 0.170, Claude Sonnet 4.6 0.169).

rows.subject: 21 LLMs (aggregate result reported across the model panel)
rows.size_stated: 21 models spanning several families; sizes vary and include open-weight parameter counts and estimated counts for closed models
rows.stage_stated: instruct for the named instruct/chat models; otherwise not stated
rows.operation_detail: Rate words on 14 explicitly named grounding dimensions and compare model ratings with human norms; examine alignment against model scale.
rows.measure: Mean Pearson r between model and human ratings, averaged across 14 dimensions; the authors report that alignment improves substantially with model scale.
rows.baseline: Estimated human ceiling about 0.89 in the main text; Appendix F gives a cross-dimension mean ceiling of about 0.78.
rows.value: Strongest model reaches Mean r ≈ 0.76 in the main text; Appendix D identifies Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 0.760 and describes scale gains as occurring on only a subset of components.
rows.uncertainty: not stated for the aggregate scale trend; Table 6 provides individual model values without uncertainty estimates.
rows.note: The overall rating result improves with scale according to the authors, but the component results are not uniformly scale-sensitive: sensory and magnitude change within some families, while internal and social are described as essentially flat and motor as a persistent weakness.
rows.check: For the measured quantity (Mean r across 14 dimensions), the authors state that alignment improves substantially with scale and fit a saturating curve (r≈0.74), so the state should be observed rather than partial. Component unevenness is a separate result and should be its own rows (see missing). The baseline is inconsistent: the main text gives a ceiling of 0.89, Appendix F gives a cross-dimension mean of 0.78.

relationships.condition: Spontaneous abstract property generation (Experiments 1 and 2), 21 models, cross-family and within-family
relationships.reason: Alignment shows no reliable or monotonic rise with parameter count, and within some families larger models score lower (r1, r2).
relationships.display_finding: Across 21 models, alignment showed no reliable or monotonic increase with parameter count, and larger models scored lower within some families.

relationships.condition: Explicit rating task on 14 grounding dimensions, Mean r
relationships.reason: Mean r rises with scale along a saturating fit, from 0.297 (Gemma 3 4B) to 0.760 (Claude Sonnet 4.6) (r3).
relationships.display_finding: Mean rating correlation followed a saturating size trend, increasing from 0.297 for Gemma 3 4B to 0.760 for Claude Sonnet 4.6.

relationships.condition: Rating task, per-component scores (from text, Appendix D Table 6)
relationships.reason: From the text, not a row: Sensory improves within families, but Internal and Social are flat and Motor does not improve or drops (Llama 0.528→0.495; Qwen3 0.540→0.375). Linked to r3 as the nearest row.
relationships.display_finding: Sensory scores improved within families, Internal and Social stayed flat, and Motor failed to improve or fell, including Llama 0.528→0.495 and Qwen3 0.540→0.375.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Alignment does not reliably rise with parameter count in Experiment 1 and has no monotonic parameter-count trend in Experiment 2 (r1–r2).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that human alignment improves substantially with scale when dimensions are explicitly named, although the component-level pattern is uneven (r3).
